newsitem.title: UK: Demand rises for UK-Australia air cargo capacity.
newsitem.headline: Demand rises for UK-Australia air cargo capacity.

text.p: Airlines report an unexpected summer upsurge in demand for their UK-to-Australia cargo services after experiencing a downward business spiral on the route in the spring, a Reuters survey shows.
And this, they note, is despite the strong pound's perceived negative effect on exports and the fact that August is a traditional off-season for airfreight.
Peak passenger period baggage is restricting cargo loads that are further diminished by factory closedowns for staff holidays.
"Nevertheless, demand is outstripping supply for ex-UK capacity to all of our Australian destinations," said Ivor Llewellyn, north UK cargo manager of Cathay Pacific Airways.

"We are filling all the space we have been allocated but we can't obtain any more capacity because the rates we charge in the UK are lower than those from the Far East, which gets space priority(from Hong Kong). The situation is critical," he said.
The increased demand has seen the average per kg/100 kg rate on the London-Sydney route increase four pence since July 14 to 1.89 stg.
Llewellyn said Cathay has a 23 percent share of the Britain-Australia airfreight market but was unable to explain the upturn in Australia business.
Thai Airways International, another carrier to experience a boom in UK-Australia cargo demand over recent weeks, also cannot pinpoint a reason.
"It is not just Britain, it is the whole of Europe that has seen a sudden, recent big increase in demand for (capacity to) Australia," said Mike Miller, Thai's UK cargo manager.

"London-Australia has always been an up-and-down market and it now looks as we are headed for a peak period," he said, adding that the carrier is likely to increase its ex-UK-Australia rates from October 1.
Qantas Airways' UK freight manager Graham Chamberlain agreed that the market in question was buoyant at what was normally a quiet time of the year for cargo.

"Add that to the strength of sterling against the Australian dollar and it's a strange scenario. I wouldn't have thought that the market could be so strong as it is at the present time, but long may it continue" he said.
Korean Air started a weekly MD-11 Seoul-Sydney freighter service in April and a cargo official in London said the Australian market badly needed extra capacity.
Most carriers operating from Britain admit, although not publicly, that they are holding back on any autumn/winter rate increase decisions until they first learn of British Airways' plans.
Some have expressed dismay at a new offer by BA of discounted pallet prices to the Far and Middle East.

A feeling commonly expressed within the London Heathrow air cargo community is that BA concentrates on pallets because its ability to handle loose freight is impaired until the opening of its new World Cargocentre at the airport in January 1999.
"BA's new flat pallet rates are 30 to 50 percent below those being charged by most other carriers," said the UK cargo manager of one major Asian airline.
Ray Dissan, UK/Ireland cargo manager of Emirates said "I just don't know why BA is selling so low. They are out of touch with the marketplace."
Air cargo trading from Britain to Japan is presently "strong", according to Cathay's Llewellyn,
"The demand for capacity is not as critical as it is for Australia, but it is still heavy. We have managed to obtain some additional space," he said.
A Japan Airlines London-based cargo official said that the London-Tokyo market was currently quite busy.
"We hit our target for July and we are scheduled (to do the same for) August." he said.
The upturn in UK-Korea air cargo fortunes, which began in June after a six-month slump, appears to be continuing.

"The demand is there, there is no doubt about that," said Cathay's Llewellyn. "Our trouble again is getting sufficient space (ex-Hong Kong), which is dominated by Asian stations that generate higher rates," he added.
The KAL UK cargo official said he expected the London-Seoul boom trend would continue. "Sterling's strength doesn't seem to have affected business," he said.
Emirates is now operating twice-weekly Dubai-Hong Kong freighter flights with 747-200Fs wet-leased from Atlas Air and these, along with daily 777 services on the route, connect with the UK.
"There is a tremendous amount of tonnage flying from Britain to Hong Kong. We have gained a certain percentage and it's growing," said Dissan.
The UK-HK route is completely new to Thai International, said Mike Miller.
"And we won't be marketing it until our new winter schedule comes into effect from October 1. I don't like bringing new destinations on mid-stream until a new tariff list is effective," he stressed.
Cathay's Llewellyn said that during July and so far in August, his airline had seen a slight slowdown in its UK-HK cargo business, which it had expected during a traditional trough period.
"But it has not slowed as much as it used to at this time of the year." he said.

Air cargo prices to China are rather low compared to Korea and Japan but KAL had nevertheless been trying to develop the China market in Britain and expects a steady growth in business, said its London official.
From Britain, Thai International is flying 170 tonnes a week to Shanghai, a market in which it has built up a 10 percent share, and 200 tonnes to the more competitively served Beijing, noted Miller.

"We are getting good London-China business right now and can see a rate rise in October. We are also doing well to Guangzhou, a route on which we have won a 25 percent market share from the UK," he said.
He added it was still to early to assess what, if any, impact Thailand's de facto devaluation of the baht in early July will have on ex-UK air cargo trading.
"What we do know is that it is going strong now," stated Miller.

As for Manila, Philippine Airlines' Keith O'Callaghan continues to be irked at his lack of capacity. This is caused by PAL's A340s taking aboard extra fuel at the expense of cargo in order to divert to Cebu during bad weather instead of Clark, located much closer to Manila.
He thought that fuel/weather circumstances, coupled with the passenger peak season, would probably last until the autumn, when more freight space should become available.
Singapore Airlines' UK cargo manager Barry Gibson said that overall, his ex-UK business to Singapore and other destinations was buoyant and was not being affected much by strong sterling.
"This probably reflects that export orders are placed long in advance and deliveries are only now on their way through the system," he said.
Bearing in mind this long lead-time, Gibson expressed concern about what impact the strong pound might be having on exports by the end of 1997.

Pakistan International Airlines' UK cargo marketing spokesman Nasim Rahimtoola told Reuters that Singapore continued to be a very crowded market of which, from Britain, his carrier had only a small share.
Emirates' Dissan described Singapore, in which his carrier had built up a "very good" ex-UK market share, as "buoyant" and a location that was fast developing as a major operating hub.
He also said Indonesia was a good, fast growing market from Britain, although one of his problems was obtaining sufficient capacity.
To Surabaya, a fairly new destination for Thai International, Mike Miller said an ex-UK rate increase could be expected from October.
"Despite the strength of sterling, there is a lot of loyalty to the UK in the UAE," said Ray Dissan."Britain's message of delivering quality goods on time is getting through to UAE buyers," he added.
But he warned that the growth of air services into Dubai exceeded cargo demand and so competition was "extremely fierce".
Air India's lack of ex-UK air cargo capacity since last year has caused a London-India space shortage, said Dissan.
"Because rates on this route were always very cheap, in the past we tended not to bother with it. But due to the shortage, people have been approaching us with business," he commented.

"We turn away more than we can carry but we do accept mainly dense traffic and, because of the space shortage, rates on the route have gone up," he said. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
